Base directory for this skill: /Users/yehor/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.4.1/skills/test-driven-development

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

**"Other tests" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A
green run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call
the change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,
`npm test`, `cargo test` — whatever the repo uses) even when your task
named only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the
deliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows —
including one you didn't cause — goes in your report by name; a red
test you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified
by omission.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
| "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

24

26	
27	**Tier 1 — core**
28	Ingest, editor, claim verification from the session record and diff, grounded script, voice, data-driven scenes, render, durable runner, CLI.
29	
30	**Tier 2 — product**
31	Web app (run view, reel page with evidence panel, inbox, gallery, landing), self-review loop, neatlogs runtime read-back and detections, budget gate from the business plan, evaluation harness and scorecard, deployment.

37	Private repositories and GitHub App auth. Agents other than those Entire records. Auto-posting to social networks (the app drafts, a human posts). Editing the user's code.
38

40	
41	One TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces), one Docker image that runs both the web app and the worker, one SQLite database and one data directory on a volume.
42	
43	```
44	apps/web           Next.js: landing, app UI, API routes, SSE progress stream
45	packages/core      shared types and zod schemas, ids, config, budget, redaction
46	packages/ingest    git + Entire checkpoint reader -> normalized sessions
47	packages/agent     model router, agent loop, tools, tracing and steering wiring
48	packages/verify    claim extraction, verifiers, grounding gate
49	packages/voice     text-to-speech and timing
50	packages/reel      Remotion scenes, composition, render API
51	packages/pipeline  stages and the durable runner
52	packages/cli       `dailies` binary and the `entire-dailies` plugin shim

63

65	
66	```
67	ingest -> edit -> verify -> script -> ground -> voice -> footage -> render -> review -> gate -> publish
68	                                ^                                              |
69	                                +---------- re-cut (at most 2 loops) ----------+

71

75	
76	| Table | Holds |
77	|---|---|
78	| `repos` | URL, default branch, last checkpoint covered, stored preferences |
79	| `runs` | repo, window, status, cost so far, budget, trace id |
80	| `stages` | run, name, status, attempt, timings, artifact path, error |
81	| `claims` | run, session, quote, kind, verdict, evidence refs |
82	| `lines` | run, scene, narration text, evidence refs, audio path, duration |
83	| `reels` | run, video path, subtitles, poster, status (draft / approved / published) |
84	| `feedback` | repo, reel, free text, resulting preference |
85	| `events` | run, timestamp, stage, message (drives the live progress stream) |
86	
87	Artifacts (cloned repos, stage JSON, audio, frames, MP4) live under one data directory behind a small storage interface.
88	
89	## 4. Stages
90	
91	**4.1 Ingest (deterministic)**
92	Partial-clone the repo, fetch `refs/entire/*` and the legacy `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch if present. For each checkpoint read `metadata.json`, the per-session metadata, `prompt.txt` and the compact `transcript.jsonl`. Map checkpoints to commits through the `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer. Select sessions inside the window. Redact secrets before anything else sees the text (key patterns, env assignments, high-entropy strings). Output: normalized `Session[]` with typed entries (user prompt, assistant text, tool call, tool result) and stable entry ids.
93	
94	Optional enrichments through the Entire CLI when it works on the clone: `entire checkpoint explain --json`, `entire graph diff|impact`, `entire dispatch --local`. Each is reported as `used` or `skipped`; nothing is invented when one is unavailable.
95	
96	**4.2 Edit (agent)**
97	Transcripts do not fit in context, so the editor navigates them with tools: `list_sessions`, `read_entries(session, range)`, `search_transcript(query)`, `get_diff(sha, path)`, `graph_impact(symbol)`. It returns at most six beats for the default 75-second target. A beat names its kind (feature, fix, decision, failure, recovery), the sessions and entry ranges it rests on and the commits involved.
98	
99	**4.3 Verify**
100	Extract the claims the coding agent made, then judge each one.
101	
102	Extraction: a small model reads assistant messages at turn ends and returns claims with the exact quote and the entry id. A claim is kept only if its quote is found in that entry (compared after collapsing whitespace and Markdown marks).
103	
104	| Claim kind | Evidence | Verdict rule |
105	|---|---|---|
106	| `tests_pass` | last test-runner call in the session before the claim, and its output | verified if it passed; contradicted if it failed; stale if code was edited after the last passing run; unverifiable if no run exists |
107	| `build_passes` | same for build, type-check and lint commands | same |
108	| `ran_command` | a matching tool call and its result | verified if it succeeded; contradicted if it errored; unverifiable if no matching call is recorded |
109	| `fixed_error` | the error text in an earlier tool result and a later run of the same command without it | unverifiable when no later run exists |
110	| `implemented` | the diff of the linked commits | a second model must quote the supporting hunk; the quote is validated against the diff |
111	
112	The first four are decided by deterministic parsers over the recorded tool results. Only `implemented` uses a model, from a different model family than the writer, and its quoted evidence is checked mechanically.
113	
114	**4.4 Script**
115	The writer produces a storyboard: ordered scenes with typed props and narration lines. The reel follows one arc: the problem (the human's request), the key decisions, the implementation, and the recorded validation. Each line carries evidence refs. Contradicted and stale claims become flag scenes. Unverifiable claims are either left out or stated as unverified.
116	
117	**4.5 Ground (gate, in code)**
118	For every line: evidence refs must resolve; every number in the sentence must appear in the facts computed for that scene; a second model must find the sentence entailed by the evidence. A failing line is rewritten up to twice, then dropped. A style lint (banned phrases, sentence length) runs here too. The on-screen text and narration are scanned again for secrets. The stage reports how many lines were dropped.
119	
120	**4.6 Voice**
121	Gemini text-to-speech per line, cached by content hash. Measured durations drive the timeline. On failure: retry with backoff, then an alternate voice, then a captions-only cut that is labelled as such.
122	
123	**4.7 Footage**
124	Scenes are rendered from data: title, quoted prompt, terminal replay, animated diff, stats, claim-versus-record flag, end card. Tier 3 adds a session timeline, the dependency-graph scene and a Playwright recording of the live app when the repo declares a URL.
125	
126	**4.8 Render**
127	Remotion composes the storyboard into 1080p30 MP4, an SRT file and a poster frame.
128	
129	**4.9 Review (agent)**
130	Deterministic checks first: total duration against target, silent gaps, black frames, per-scene text limits. Findings map to fixes (shorten a line, change scene parameters, regenerate audio) and the run loops back, at most twice.
131	
132	**4.10 Gate (in code)**
133	All must hold: grounding passed, secret scan clean, review passed, cost within budget, human approval recorded. Failure of any condition blocks publishing; there is no override path in the worker.
134	
135	**4.11 Publish**
136	Mark the reel public, write the evidence page, draft a post for the human to send, and, on repositories the owner has authorised, comment the link on the pull request or commit.
137	
138	## 5. Human loop
139	
140	The reel page offers **Approve** and **Request changes** with free text. Feedback is stored as a per-repo preference and passed to the editor and writer on the next run; a re-cut reruns from `script` with the feedback attached.
141	
142	## 6. Integrations
143	
144	### Entire
145	- **Input.** Checkpoints are the product's only source of truth about what the agents did. Reading goes through plain git refs so that any public repo works without credentials.
146	- **Plugin.** `entire-dailies` on PATH makes `entire dailies` run the same engine locally: `entire dailies --since 24h`, `entire dailies verify` (claims table only, no video).
147	- **Write-back.** The reel link is attached to the pull request or commit.
148	
149	### neatlogs
150	- **Tracing.** One trace per run. Root span is the workflow, child spans per stage, agent spans for editor, extractor, judge, writer and reviewer, tool spans per tool call, guardrail spans per gate carrying pass/fail and reasons. The run id is the session id.
151	- **Runtime read-back (MCP).** At run start the agent searches its earlier traces for the same repo and carries forward what failed last time. Nightly it reads project analytics into `business/actuals.json`. At boot it creates detections for gate failures, repeated render retries and dropped lines.
152	- **neatroots.** Runs beside the agent during development and evaluation with the checks in `.neatroots/checks/`; the editor and writer get the `check_my_work` tool through steering. Whether it also runs beside the production worker is decided after a spike; if not, the README says so.
153	
154	### cfo.ai
155	- The business plan (pricing, cost of a reel, revenue, runway) lives in cfo.ai and is exported to `business/plan.json`.
156	- `pnpm budget:sync` turns the plan's price and target margin into `budget.generated.ts` (maximum cost per reel, per stage). The gate enforces it.
157	- `pnpm actuals:push` writes measured cost per reel from traces for the plan-versus-actual view.
158	
159	### Models
160	OpenAI-compatible client with a router. Roles map to models: editor and writer on a Claude Sonnet model, extractor on a small Claude model, entailment and `implemented` judge on a Nova model, vision on a Claude Sonnet model. Provider order: the hackathon gateway, then Venice on rate-limit, budget or server errors. A rate limiter stays under the gateway's 60 requests per minute. A per-run meter stops the run when the budget is reached.
161	
162	### Hosting
163	One Docker image with Node, git, the Entire CLI, Chromium and ffmpeg. Target is Fly.io or Railway with a volume; the choice is made at deploy time and nothing in the code depends on it.
164	
165	## 7. Surfaces
166	
167	| Route | Purpose |
168	|---|---|
169	| `/` | Landing: one claim, one call to action, a real reel playing |
170	| `/new` | Paste a repository URL, choose a window |
171	| `/r/[run]` | Live run: stages, events, cost so far |
172	| `/reel/[id]` | Player, evidence panel (each line and its sources), flags, cost, trace reference |
173	| `/inbox` | Reels waiting for approval or feedback |
174	| `/gallery` | Published reels |
175	| `/economics` | Plan versus actual cost per reel |
176	| `/health` | Evaluation scorecard, detections, open fixes for the agent itself |
177	
178	Viewing is public. Starting a run is rate-limited per address and capped per day because every run costs money. Approving requires the owner token.
179	
180	CLI: `dailies run <repo|path> [--since 24h] [--no-render] [--out dir]`, `dailies verify <repo|path>`.
181	
182	## 8. Failure handling
183	
184	| Failure | Response |
185	|---|---|
186	| Repo has no checkpoints | Run ends early with a clear message; nothing is rendered |
187	| Model rate limit or server error | Backoff, then the fallback provider |
188	| Budget reached mid-run | Run stops in `blocked`, partial artifacts kept |
189	| Text-to-speech fails | Retry, alternate voice, then captions-only cut labelled as such |
190	| Render crashes | Retry the stage from its inputs; storyboard and audio are reused |
191	| Review still failing after two loops | Run ends in `blocked` with the findings attached |
192	| Process restart | Unfinished runs resume from the last completed stage |
193	| Entire CLI enrichment unavailable | Marked `skipped`; the run continues on git data |
194	
195	## 9. Evaluation
196	
197	- **Mutation benchmark.** For every verified `tests_pass` or `build_passes` claim, flip the recorded tool result to a failure; the verdict must become contradicted. For every contradicted one, flip it to a pass; the verdict must become verified. This shows a green verdict is never vacuous.
198	- **Grounding benchmark.** Inject fabricated narration lines (wrong numbers, features absent from the diff) next to true ones. The gate must reject all fabricated lines and keep the true ones.
199	- **Field sample.** Run the verifier over sessions from public repositories pinned by commit. Hand-label a sample of flagged claims; the labels' hash is committed before the run. Report precision. Results are aggregate; no repository is named.
200	- **Baseline comparison.** The same sessions through a single-prompt summariser with no gates versus the full pipeline: unsupported statements per reel, tokens and cost.
201	
202	Scorecards are committed as JSON and Markdown, failures included.
203	
204	## 10. Testing
205	
206	Unit tests for the parsers (checkpoint reader, test-runner output, trailer mapping), verifiers, grounding gate, redaction, budget and the runner's resume logic, written test-first. Fixture checkpoints are small synthetic trees built in the tests. One end-to-end test runs the pipeline with a mock model and a stub renderer.
207	
208	## 11. Privacy and safety
209	
210	Only public repositories. Redaction runs at ingest and again at the gate, and the gate fails closed. Reels about a repository are unlisted until its owner approves. Evaluation statistics about other people's repositories are published only in aggregate.
211	
212	## 12. Known limits
213	
214	- Verification rests on what the session recorded. A command the agent ran outside the recorded session is invisible.
215	- `implemented` claims rely on a model's judgement, constrained by a quoted, validated hunk.
216	- The voice is synthetic.
217	- Session formats other than Claude Code's are parsed best-effort.

- **Plugin.** `entire-dailies` on PATH makes `entire dailies` run the same engine locally: `entire dailies --since 24h`, `entire dailies verify` (claims table only, no video).
- **Write-back.** The reel link is attached to the pull request or commit.

### neatlogs
- **Tracing.** One trace per run. Root span is the workflow, child spans per stage, agent spans for editor, extractor, judge, writer and reviewer, tool spans per tool call, guardrail spans per gate carrying pass/fail and reasons. The run id is the session id.
- **Runtime read-back (MCP).** At run start the agent searches its earlier traces for the same repo and carries forward what failed last time. Nightly it reads project analytics into `business/actuals.json`. At boot it creates detections for gate failures, repeated render retries and dropped lines.
- **neatroots.** Runs beside the agent during development and evaluation with the checks in `.neatroots/checks/`; the editor and writer get the `check_my_work` tool through steering. Whether it also runs beside the production worker is decided after a spike; if not, the README says so.

### cfo.ai
- The business plan (pricing, cost of a reel, revenue, runway) lives in cfo.ai and is exported to `business/plan.json`.
- `pnpm budget:sync` turns the plan's price and target margin into `budget.generated.ts` (maximum cost per reel, per stage). The gate enforces it.
- `pnpm actuals:push` writes measured cost per reel from traces for the plan-versus-actual view.

### Models
OpenAI-compatible client with a router. Roles map to models: editor and writer on a Claude Sonnet model, extractor on a small Claude model, entailment and `implemented` judge on a Nova model, vision on a Claude Sonnet model. Provider order: the hackathon gateway, then Venice on rate-limit, budget or server errors. A rate limiter stays under the gateway's 60 requests per minute. A per-run meter stops the run when the budget is reached.

### Hosting
One Docker image with Node, git, the Entire CLI, Chromium and ffmpeg. Target is Fly.io or Railway with a volume; the choice is made at deploy time and nothing in the code depends on it.

## 7. Surfaces

| Route | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/` | Landing: one claim, one call to action, a real reel playing |
| `/new` | Paste a repository URL, choose a window |
| `/r/[run]` | Live run: stages, events, cost so far |
| `/reel/[id]` | Player, evidence panel (each line and its sources), flags, cost, trace reference |
| `/inbox` | Reels waiting for approval or feedback |
| `/gallery` | Published reels |
| `/economics` | Plan versus actual cost per reel |
| `/health` | Evaluation scorecard, detections, open fixes for the agent itself |

Viewing is public. Starting a run is rate-limited per address and capped per day because every run costs money. Approving requires the owner token.

CLI: `dailies run <repo|path> [--since 24h] [--no-render] [--out dir]`, `dailies verify <repo|path>`.

## 8. Failure handling

| Failure | Response |
|---|---|
| Repo has no checkpoints | Run ends early with a clear message; nothing is rendered |
| Model rate limit or server error | Backoff, then the fallback provider |
| Budget reached mid-run | Run stops in `blocked`, partial artifacts kept |
| Text-to-speech fails | Retry, alternate voice, then captions-only cut labelled as such |
| Render crashes | Retry the stage from its inputs; storyboard and audio are reused |
| Review still failing after two loops | Run ends in `blocked` with the findings attached |
| Process restart | Unfinished runs resume from the last completed stage |
| Entire CLI enrichment unavailable | Marked `skipped`; the run continues on git data |

## 9. Evaluation

- **Mutation benchmark.** For every verified `tests_pass` or `build_passes` claim, flip the recorded tool result to a failure; the verdict must become contradicted. For every contradicted one, flip it to a pass; the verdict must become verified. This shows a green verdict is never vacuous.
- **Grounding benchmark.** Inject fabricated narration lines (wrong numbers, features absent from the diff) next to true ones. The gate must reject all fabricated lines and keep the true ones.
- **Field sample.** Run the verifier over sessions from public repositories pinned by commit. Hand-label a sample of flagged claims; the labels' hash is committed before the run. Report precision. Results are aggregate; no repository is named.
- **Baseline comparison.** The same sessions through a single-prompt summariser with no gates versus the full pipeline: unsupported statements per reel, tokens and cost.

Scorecards are committed as JSON and Markdown, failures included.

## 10. Testing

Unit tests for the parsers (checkpoint reader, test-runner output, trailer mapping), verifiers, grounding gate, redaction, budget and the runner's resume logic, written test-first. Fixture checkpoints are small synthetic trees built in the tests. One end-to-end test runs the pipeline with a mock model and a stub renderer.

## 11. Privacy and safety

Only public repositories. Redaction runs at ingest and again at the gate, and the gate fails closed. Reels about a repository are unlisted until its owner approves. Evaluation statistics about other people's repositories are published only in aggregate.

## 12. Known limits

- Verification rests on what the session recorded. A command the agent ran outside the recorded session is invisible.
- `implemented` claims rely on a model's judgement, constrained by a quoted, validated hunk.
- The voice is synthetic.
- Session formats other than Claude Code's are parsed best-effort.

1094	
1095	1. **Rendering speed is a deployment setting.** A 30-second reel renders in 35 seconds on a laptop and in 145 seconds on the 4-core server, which has no graphics card. `renderReel` reads two optional environment variables: `DAILIES_RENDER_CONCURRENCY` (an integer passed to the renderer as its concurrency; default left to the renderer) and `DAILIES_RENDER_SCALE` (a number between 0.25 and 1 passed as the output scale, so 0.667 yields 1280x720 from the same composition; default 1). Invalid values are ignored with a logged warning. Test both through an injected environment object, without rendering.
1096	   (An earlier note here blamed the working directory for render timeouts. That was wrong. The cause was macOS: a browser binary stored under a privacy-protected folder stops producing frames when the screen locks. `DAILIES_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` already lets a render use a binary elsewhere.)
1097	2. **Home directories on screen.** Recorded tool output contains paths such as `/Users/<name>/…`, `/home/<name>/…` and `C:\Users\<name>\…`, and they end up in terminal scenes. `redact` replaces the home prefix with `~` (counted separately from secret hits, so the gate's secret check is unaffected). Test with all three forms.
1098	3. **No spans per stage.** A run's trace shows model and tool calls but not the stages, and a run that ended `failed` showed as a successful trace. Wrap every stage in a `CHAIN` span named after the stage, inside which a thrown error marks the span as failed; record on the root span the final status, reason and cost.
1099	4. **Earlier runs are recalled but not used.** `recallRepo` exists and nothing calls it. Call it once at the start of the edit stage, log `memory: <n> earlier runs, <m> with failures` (or `memory: skipped, <reason>`), and append the notes to the editor's and the writer's prompts under a heading that marks them as history, not instructions.
1100	5. **A re-cut of an approved reel stays approved.** While the new cut is rendering, the old approval still stands. `recut` through the feedback route sets the reel back to draft.
1101	6. **The default budget is below a real run.** A real 12-session run costs about $0.60 after the editor fix. `DEFAULT_BUDGET.maxCostPerReelUsd` becomes 1.0 until the business plan sets it.
1102	7. **The review stage is built and never runs.** `reviewStage` is not exported as a function from `@dailies/pipeline`, so neither the command-line tool nor the worker can place it before the gate, and `--no-review` does nothing. Export it, insert it between `render` and `gate` in both entry points, and make `--no-review` leave it out. 1. **Rendering speed is a deployment setting.** A 30-second reel renders in 35 seconds on a laptop and in 145 seconds on the 4-core server, which has no graphics card. `renderReel` reads two optional environment variables: `DAILIES_RENDER_CONCURRENCY` (an integer passed to the renderer as its concurrency; default left to the renderer) and `DAILIES_RENDER_SCALE` (a number between 0.25 and 1 passed as the output scale, so 0.667 yields 1280x720 from the same composition; default 1). Invalid values are ignored with a logged warning. Test both through an injected environment object, without rendering.
   (An earlier note here blamed the working directory for render timeouts. That was wrong. The cause was macOS: a browser binary stored under a privacy-protected folder stops producing frames when the screen locks. `DAILIES_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` already lets a render use a binary elsewhere.)
2. **Home directories on screen.** Recorded tool output contains paths such as `/Users/<name>/…`, `/home/<name>/…` and `C:\Users\<name>\…`, and they end up in terminal scenes. `redact` replaces the home prefix with `~` (counted separately from secret hits, so the gate's secret check is unaffected). Test with all three forms.
3. **No spans per stage.** A run's trace shows model and tool calls but not the stages, and a run that ended `failed` showed as a successful trace. Wrap every stage in a `CHAIN` span named after the stage, inside which a thrown error marks the span as failed; record on the root span the final status, reason and cost.
4. **Earlier runs are recalled but not used.** `recallRepo` exists and nothing calls it. Call it once at the start of the edit stage, log `memory: <n> earlier runs, <m> with failures` (or `memory: skipped, <reason>`), and append the notes to the editor's and the writer's prompts under a heading that marks them as history, not instructions.
5. **A re-cut of an approved reel stays approved.** While the new cut is rendering, the old approval still stands. `recut` through the feedback route sets the reel back to draft.
6. **The default budget is below a real run.** A real 12-session run costs about $0.60 after the editor fix. `DEFAULT_BUDGET.maxCostPerReelUsd` becomes 1.0 until the business plan sets it.
7. **The review stage is built and never runs.** `reviewStage` is not exported as a function from `@dailies/pipeline`, so neither the command-line tool nor the worker can place it before the gate, and `--no-review` does nothing. Export it, insert it between `render` and `gate` in both entry points, and make `--no-review` leave it out. Test: the stage list of a default run contains `review` immediately before `gate`, and the list with `--no-review` does not.

/**
 * Neatlogs OpenRouter Agent integration.
 *
 * Wraps the `@openrouter/agent` SDK so each `client.callModel(...)` is traced.
 * The OpenRouter client returns a `ModelResult`; telemetry is finalized when the
 * result is consumed (via `getText()` / awaiting it / iterating it), matching the
 * SDK's lazy-evaluation model — a result that is never consumed ships no span.
 *
 * Usage:
 *   import { init } from 'neatlogs';
 *   import { wrapOpenRouterAgent } from 'neatlogs/openrouter-agent';
 *   import { OpenRouter } from '@openrouter/agent';
 *
 *   await init({ apiKey, workflowName });
 *   const openrouter = wrapOpenRouterAgent(new OpenRouter({ apiKey: process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY }));
 *   const result = openrouter.callModel({ model: 'openai/gpt-4o', messages: [...] });
 *   const text = await result.getText();
 *
 * Also exports wrapCallModel() for the standalone callModel helper:
 *   const trackedCallModel = wrapCallModel(callModel);
 *   const result = trackedCallModel(openrouter, { model, messages });
 */
/**
 * Wrap an OpenRouter client instance so `callModel` emits LLM spans. Returns a
 * Proxy over the client; all other methods pass through unchanged.
 */
declare function wrapOpenRouterAgent<T extends object>(client: T): T;
/**
 * Wrap the standalone `callModel(client, opts)` helper. The wrapped function is
 * invoked with the client passed in: `trackedCallModel(openrouter, {...})`.
 */
declare function wrapCallModel<F extends (...args: any[]) => any>(callModel: F): F;

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.
